result.target_topic: Stock-Based Compensation Valuation and Expense Recognition Methodology
result.target_summary: The company uses the closing trading price minus a dividend yield discount for RSUs and corporate-target PSUs, Monte Carlo simulation for market-based PSUs, and the Black-Scholes model for ESPP. Compensation expense for RSUs and market-based PSUs is recognized on a straight-line basis, while expense for PSUs and ESPP is recognized using an accelerated amortization model.

This is absent in the 2024 text provided. Additionally, the 2025 disclosure clarifies that the accelerated amortization for 'PSUs' applies specifically to 'non-market PSUs... based on performance targets probable of achievement,' refining the broader 2024 description. This adds a specific quantification methodology (forfeiture estimation) previously not detailed in this summary/evidence block.

comparisons.peer_topic: Stock-based compensation valuation models and expense recognition policy
comparisons.peer_summary: The Company uses the Black-Scholes and Monte Carlo simulation models to estimate the fair value of stock options, RSUs, and ESPP shares at the grant date. Compensation expense is generally recognized using the straight-line method over the vesting period, with forfeitures estimated at grant and revised if necessary.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AMD use Monte Carlo simulation for market-based performance stock units and Black-Scholes for ESPP. However, NVDA applies an accelerated amortization model for PSU and ESPP expense recognition, whereas AMD generally uses the straight-line method for most awards, including RSUs and ESPP, with specific ratable recognition only for RSUs with performance or market conditions. NVDA also explicitly details the dividend yield discount for RSUs/PSUs, while AMD uses the closing grant-date price for standard RSUs.

sentences.text: We use a Monte Carlo simulation on the date of grant to estimate the fair value of performance stock units that are based on market conditions, or market-based PSUs.

The compensation expense for RSUs and market-based PSUs is recognized using a straight-line attribution method over the requisite employee service period while compensation expense for PSUs is recognized using an accelerated amortization model.

We estimate the fair value of shares to be issued under our employee stock purchase plan, or ESPP, using the Black-Scholes model at the commencement of an offering period in March and September of each year.
Stock-based compensation for our ESPP is expensed using an accelerated amortization model.
The Company estimates the grant-date fair value of RSUs that involve a market condition using the Monte Carlo simulation model.
The Company estimates the grant-date fair value of stock to be issued under the Company's Employee Stock Purchase plan (ESPP) using the Black-Scholes model.

Compensation expense is recognized over the vesting period of the applicable award using the straight-line method, except for the compensation expense related to RSUs with performance or market conditions (PRSUs), which are recognized ratably for each vesting tranche from the service inception date to the end of the requisite service period.

comparisons.peer_topic: Stock-based compensation for RSUs and options
comparisons.peer_summary: Broadcom recognizes compensation expense for time-based RSUs using straight-line amortization based on grant-date fair value, and for stock options and ESPP rights using the Black-Scholes model with straight-line amortization.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies use the straight-line amortization method for RSUs based on grant-date fair value adjusted for dividends. AVGO explicitly reduces fair value by the present value of dividends, whereas NVDA reduces the closing trading price by a dividend yield discount. Both use Black-Scholes for ESPP, though NVDA uses an accelerated amortization model for ESPP expense while AVGO uses straight-line amortization for ESPP.

sentences.text: We use the closing trading price of our common stock on the date of grant, minus a dividend yield discount, as the fair value of awards of restricted stock units, or RSUs, and performance stock units that are based on our corporate financial performance targets, or PSUs.

We estimate the fair value of shares to be issued under our employee stock purchase plan, or ESPP, using the Black-Scholes model at the commencement of an offering period in March and September of each year.
Stock-based compensation for our ESPP is expensed using an accelerated amortization model.
We recognize compensation expense for time-based restricted stock units ("RSUs") using the straight-line amortization method based on the fair value of RSUs on the date of grant.

The fair value of RSUs is the closing market price of Broadcom common stock on the date of grant, reduced by the present value of dividends expected to be paid on Broadcom common stock prior to vesting.

We recognize compensation expense for time-based stock options and employee stock purchase plan rights under the Broadcom Inc. Employee Stock Purchase Plan, as amended ("ESPP") based on the estimated grant-date fair value determined using the Black-Scholes valuation model with a straight-line amortization method.

comparisons.peer_summary: Equity awards with market conditions have fair values estimated using Monte Carlo simulations, with compensation expense amortized using a graded vesting method over the service period.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AVGO use Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the fair value of market-based PSUs. A key difference is the expense recognition method: NVDA recognizes expense for market-based PSUs using a straight-line attribution method, whereas AVGO amortizes compensation expense for market-based awards using a graded vesting method over the service period.

sentences.text: We use a Monte Carlo simulation on the date of grant to estimate the fair value of performance stock units that are based on market conditions, or market-based PSUs.

The compensation expense for RSUs and market-based PSUs is recognized using a straight-line attribution method over the requisite employee service period while compensation expense for PSUs is recognized using an accelerated amortization model.
The fair value of market-based awards is estimated on the date of grant using the Monte Carlo simulation technique.
Compensation expense for market-based awards is amortized based upon a graded vesting method over the service period.

comparisons.peer_topic: Fair value estimation methods for equity awards
comparisons.peer_summary: The fair value of RSUs and PSUs with service or performance conditions is estimated using the common stock grant date value, reduced by the present value of expected dividends. PSUs with market conditions are valued using a Monte Carlo simulation model based on historical volatility.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and INTC use Monte Carlo simulation for PSUs with market conditions. Both use grant-date fair value reduced for expected dividends for service/performance-based RSUs and PSUs. INTC uses straight-line amortization for all share-based compensation, while NVDA uses straight-line for RSUs/market PSUs but accelerated amortization for corporate PSUs and ESPP.

sentences.text: We use the closing trading price of our common stock on the date of grant, minus a dividend yield discount, as the fair value of awards of restricted stock units, or RSUs, and performance stock units that are based on our corporate financial performance targets, or PSUs.
We use a Monte Carlo simulation on the date of grant to estimate the fair value of performance stock units that are based on market conditions, or market-based PSUs.

The compensation expense for RSUs and market-based PSUs is recognized using a straight-line attribution method over the requisite employee service period while compensation expense for PSUs is recognized using an accelerated amortization model.

We estimate the fair value of RSUs and PSUs with a service condition or performance condition using the value of our common stock on the date of grant, reduced by the present value of dividends expected to be paid on our shares of common stock prior to vesting.
We estimate the fair value of PSUs with a market condition using a Monte Carlo simulation model as of the date of grant using historical volatility.

comparisons.peer_topic: Accounting method for stock-based compensation expense
comparisons.peer_summary: Stock-based compensation expense is measured at the grant date based on the award's fair value and recognized using the straight-line attribution method over the requisite service period.
comparisons.comparison: MU and NVDA both discuss stock-based compensation expense recognition, but MU discloses a uniform straight-line attribution method over the requisite service period. In contrast, NVDA discloses a hybrid approach, using straight-line attribution for RSUs and market-based PSUs, but an accelerated amortization model for PSUs (performance) and ESPP. MU does not detail the specific valuation models (Monte Carlo/Black-Scholes) in the cited text, whereas NVDA provides specific methodology for each award type.

sentences.text: The compensation expense for RSUs and market-based PSUs is recognized using a straight-line attribution method over the requisite employee service period while compensation expense for PSUs is recognized using an accelerated amortization model.
Stock-based compensation is measured at the grant date, based on the fair value of the award, and recognized as expense under the straight-line attribution method over the requisite service period.
